# Percutaneous Left Atrial Appendage Closure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia and a major cause of ischemic stroke, accounting for a substantial proportion of cardioembolic events [1]. Oral anticoagulation (OAC) with vitamin K antagonists (VKAs) or direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) remains the cornerstone of stroke prevention in patients with nonvalvular AF [2]. However, a significant subset of patients have contraindications to long-term anticoagulation, most often due to bleeding risk [3]. The recognition that the left atrial appendage (LAA) is the dominant source of thrombus in nonvalvular AF—accounting for roughly 90% of atrial thrombi—provided the anatomical rationale for mechanical exclusion of the appendage [4]. Percutaneous LAA closure (LAAC) has emerged as a structural alternative to lifelong anticoagulation in selected patients [5].

## Rationale and Anatomy

The LAA is a trabeculated, variably shaped outpouching of the left atrium whose morphology ("chicken wing," "windsock," "cactus," and "cauliflower") influences both thrombogenicity and procedural approach [6]. Stasis within the appendage during AF promotes thrombus formation, and surgical or percutaneous occlusion aims to eliminate this nidus [4]. Preprocedural imaging with transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) and increasingly cardiac computed tomography is essential to characterize LAA dimensions and exclude pre-existing thrombus [7].

## Devices and Procedure

Two broad device categories dominate contemporary practice. Endocardial plug-and-disc or pacifier-type devices, exemplified by the Watchman and Amplatzer Amulet families, are deployed via transseptal puncture under fluoroscopic and echocardiographic guidance [8,9]. The epicardial LARIAT system achieves ligation through a combined endocardial-epicardial approach but is less widely used [10]. Device selection and sizing depend on accurate ostial and depth measurement, and procedural success rates exceed 95% in experienced centers [11].

## Evidence from Randomized Trials

The PROTECT AF trial first demonstrated that the Watchman device was noninferior to warfarin for the composite of stroke, systemic embolism, and cardiovascular death in patients eligible for anticoagulation [12]. Longer-term follow-up confirmed durable benefit, with reductions in hemorrhagic stroke and mortality [13]. The PREVAIL trial addressed early safety concerns and, together with PROTECT AF, contributed to a patient-level meta-analysis supporting the efficacy of LAAC [14,15]. The PRAGUE-17 trial extended comparison to DOACs, showing noninferiority of LAAC versus DOACs in high-risk AF patients [16]. The Amulet IDE trial established noninferiority of the Amplatzer Amulet to the Watchman device for safety and efficacy endpoints [17].

## Real-World Registries and Outcomes

Large registries, including the EWOLUTION study and the U.S. National Cardiovascular Data Registry LAAO Registry, have confirmed high implantation success and acceptable complication rates in routine practice [18,19]. Procedural complications include pericardial effusion and tamponade, device embolization, and vascular access events, though rates have declined with operator experience and improved devices [20]. Periprocedural stroke remains uncommon but serious [21].

## Post-Procedure Management and Device-Related Thrombus

Optimal antithrombotic management following implantation remains debated. Initial protocols used warfarin followed by dual antiplatelet therapy, but DOAC-based and antiplatelet-only regimens are increasingly employed, particularly in patients with high bleeding risk [22]. Device-related thrombus (DRT) occurs in approximately 3–4% of cases and is associated with increased thromboembolic risk, prompting surveillance imaging [23]. Incomplete closure with peri-device leak has been variably associated with adverse events, and its clinical significance continues to be studied [24].

## Guidelines and Patient Selection

Current guidelines assign LAAC a role primarily in patients with nonvalvular AF and contraindications to long-term anticoagulation, reflecting the limited randomized data in this specific population [2,25]. Appropriate patient selection through multidisciplinary heart-team evaluation is emphasized [26]. Combining LAAC with other structural interventions, such as catheter ablation, has been explored to streamline care [27].

## Future Directions

Ongoing randomized trials, including CHAMPION-AF and CATALYST, are comparing LAAC directly with DOACs in broader populations and may expand indications [28]. Advances in imaging-guided sizing, including intracardiac echocardiography and computational modeling, aim to reduce complications and optimize device positioning [29]. Cost-effectiveness analyses suggest LAAC may be economically favorable over a lifetime horizon compared with warfarin and DOACs in suitable patients [30].

## Conclusion

Percutaneous LAAC is an established, evidence-supported option for stroke prevention in selected patients with nonvalvular AF, particularly those unable to tolerate long-term anticoagulation. While randomized data support noninferiority to both warfarin and DOACs in specific populations, ongoing trials will clarify its role relative to contemporary anticoagulation. Refinements in device technology, imaging, and antithrombotic management continue to improve safety and outcomes.
